title: AP Music Theory
summary: Read pitch and rhythm, analyse tonal harmony and explain musical structure.
frameworkNote: Checked against the official eight-unit sequence on 15 October 2026 for 2026-27. These original text exercises support notation and analysis. They do not replace audio dictation, sight-singing, score study or teacher feedback. Pitch names use scientific octave labels where needed.

modules.title: Count beats and spell a major scale
modules.focus: Connect pitch order to meter and beat division.
explanation: A major scale follows whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half steps. Use each letter name once before repeating the tonic. A key signature supplies consistent alterations; an accidental changes a note according to notation conventions within its measure.

Meter groups beats, while rhythm describes durations within that grouping. In simple meter a beat divides into two; in compound meter it divides into three. Six-eight commonly groups six eighth notes into two dotted-quarter beats, so counting six equal pulses alone misses the usual larger organisation.

workedExample.prompt: Spell D major and identify the usual beats in 6/8.
steps: Apply the step pattern: D E F-sharp G A B C-sharp D.
Group the six eighth notes as 3 + 3, giving two dotted-quarter beats.

misconception.claim: The top meter number always equals the number of felt beats.
misconception.correction: Compound meter commonly groups three subdivisions into each beat.

questions.hint: The fourth scale degree requires an accidental.
questions.answer: F G A B-flat C D E F.

questions.prompt: How many eighth notes fit one dotted quarter?
questions.hint: A dot adds half the original value.
questions.answer: Three eighth notes: two for the quarter plus one for its dot.

modules.title: Distinguish minor forms and textures
modules.focus: Track altered scale degrees and independent lines.
explanation: Natural minor has lowered third, sixth and seventh degrees relative to parallel major. Harmonic minor raises the seventh to create a leading tone. The conventional ascending melodic minor also raises the sixth; its conventional descending form returns to natural minor.

Texture concerns how musical layers relate. Monophony has one melodic line, even if doubled at the octave. Homophony often combines a principal melody with accompaniment. Polyphony involves multiple independent melodic lines. Instrument count alone cannot determine texture, and a written label still needs confirmation through score or listening evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Compare A natural minor and A harmonic minor.
steps: Write A B C D E F G A for natural minor.
Raise G to G-sharp in harmonic minor, creating a semitone approach to A.

misconception.claim: Minor always means slower or sadder music.
misconception.correction: Mode describes pitch relationships; tempo and expressive effect depend on additional choices.

questions.answer: A B C D E F-sharp G-sharp A.

questions.prompt: Ten singers perform the same melody in octaves. What texture is this?
questions.answer: Monophonic, because there is one melodic line doubled at the octave.
checkpoints: Does not infer polyphony from numbers

modules.title: Spell chords before naming inversions
modules.focus: Separate a chord’s root from its bass.
explanation: A triad stacks two thirds. A major triad combines a major third and minor third above the root; a minor triad reverses that order. A dominant seventh chord adds a minor seventh above the root of a major triad.

Inversion depends on the lowest sounding chord member, not the top note. Root position places the root in the bass; first inversion places the third there; second inversion places the fifth there. Rearranging upper voices without changing the bass does not create a new inversion.

workedExample.prompt: Name E-G-C with E as the lowest note in C major.
steps: Reorder the pitch classes as C-E-G to identify a C major triad.
E is the third in the bass, so the chord is I6, first inversion.

misconception.claim: The lowest note is always the root.
misconception.correction: In an inversion the root remains the same while another chord member is lowest.

questions.prompt: Spell a G dominant seventh chord.
questions.hint: Build a major triad and add a minor seventh.

questions.prompt: Name the inversion of C-E-A with C lowest.
questions.answer: A minor in first inversion: A-C-E with its third C in the bass.
checkpoints: Uses the bass to name inversion

modules.title: Hear function through written resolution
modules.focus: Use leading tones and chord sevenths purposefully.
explanation: In common-practice tonal harmony, tonic establishes a point of rest and dominant creates an expectation of return. At a V7-I resolution, the leading tone typically moves upward to tonic and the chordal seventh downward by step. Voice-leading rules describe this style, not every musical tradition.

Analyse each voice horizontally as well as each chord vertically. Correct chord spelling does not prevent awkward leaps, crossed voices or parallel perfect intervals. A cadence is a phrase-ending harmonic event; a perfect authentic cadence also depends on root-position V-I and tonic in the final soprano.

workedExample.prompt: Resolve the tendency tones B and F from G7 to C major.
steps: In C major B is the leading tone, so move it up to C.
F is the dominant chord’s seventh, so move it down to E.

misconception.claim: Any V-I progression is a perfect authentic cadence.
misconception.correction: Its phrase placement, inversions and final soprano also matter.

questions.prompt: Where does F normally resolve in G7-C?
questions.answer: Down by step to E in the common-practice resolution.

questions.prompt: A phrase ends on V in C major. Name the cadence.

modules.title: Prepare the dominant
explanation: Predominant harmony commonly leads toward dominant. In a major key, ii and IV often fill this role. Roman numerals show scale-degree roots and chord quality, while figured-bass symbols identify inversions. Harmonic function depends on context as well as a chord label.

A cadential six-four commonly places tonic-triad pitches above the dominant bass before V. In that context its upper notes behave as embellishments of dominant harmony: the fourth above the bass resolves to a third and the sixth to a fifth. Labelling its pitches I6/4 alone does not explain its function.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse D-F-A, G-B-D, C-E-G in C major.
steps: Identify roots D, G and C as degrees 2, 5 and 1.
Label ii-V-I and explain the progression as predominant, dominant and tonic.

misconception.claim: Every tonic triad has tonic function.
misconception.correction: A cadential six-four can serve dominant expansion because of its bass and resolutions.

questions.prompt: In C major, C and E sound over bass G before B and D over G. Describe the upper motion.
questions.answer: The fourth C moves to the third B; the sixth E moves to the fifth D.

modules.title: Identify embellishing tones
modules.focus: Use approach, departure and metric placement.
explanation: A non-chord tone is understood against the harmony sounding beneath it. A passing tone connects two chord tones by step in the same direction. A neighbour tone leaves a chord tone by step and returns to it. A suspension is prepared, held into a new harmony, then resolves, usually downward by step.

Do not label every unfamiliar note as a wrong note or identify embellishments from pitch alone. Establish the chord and track the melodic motion. Motives can also return at a new pitch level or with changed rhythm; describe what remains recognisable and what changes.

workedExample.prompt: Over a sustained C major chord, a melody plays C-D-E.
steps: C and E belong to the chord while D does not.
The melody moves by step in one direction, so D is a passing tone.

misconception.claim: Any repeated non-chord note is a suspension.
misconception.correction: A suspension requires preparation and a held note across a harmonic change before resolution.

questions.prompt: Over C major, identify D in C-D-C.
questions.hint: Look at the return to the original pitch.

questions.prompt: A short melody returns two scale steps higher with the same rhythm. What device is suggested?
questions.hint: Think of a repeated pattern at another level.
questions.answer: A melodic sequence, if the pattern is repeated at the new pitch level.

modules.title: Explain a secondary dominant
explanation: A secondary dominant is the dominant of a diatonic chord other than tonic. In C major, D major can function as V/V because D-F-sharp-A leads to G. The F-sharp acts as a local leading tone to G even though it is outside the C major key signature.

Tonicisation briefly gives a chord tonic-like emphasis. Modulation establishes a new key more durably through phrase structure and cadential evidence. One chromatic chord alone is insufficient to claim a modulation. Spell the target chord first, then build its dominant and check the actual resolution.

steps: D7 contains D-F-sharp-A-C and points toward G.
Label V7/V-V-I: G is temporarily tonicised before the phrase returns to C.

misconception.claim: Every accidental proves a change of key.
misconception.correction: Accidentals can embellish a line or create brief tonicisation without establishing a new key.

questions.hint: The target ii is D minor; find D’s dominant.
questions.answer: A C-sharp E, an A major triad.

questions.prompt: Where does F-sharp tend to move in D7-G?
questions.hint: Treat G as the local tonic.

modules.title: Compare modes and phrase designs
modules.focus: Distinguish pitch collection from formal return.
explanation: A mode has a tonic and a characteristic interval pattern. D Dorian uses D-E-F-G-A-B-C-D; its raised sixth relative to D natural minor is B-natural. Playing white notes without establishing a tonal centre does not by itself communicate a particular mode.

Form describes relationships across spans of music. In binary form two principal sections are often labelled A and B. Ternary form returns to A after a contrasting B. Repetition signs, cadences, thematic material and key areas all contribute to analysis; section length alone is not decisive.

workedExample.prompt: Compare D Dorian with D natural minor, then describe A-B-A.
steps: Only the sixth differs: Dorian has B-natural and natural minor has B-flat.
A-B-A suggests ternary organisation when the final A restores recognisable opening material.

misconception.claim: Any three phrases create ternary form.
misconception.correction: Ternary form depends on contrasting and returning material, not simply counting phrases.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes C Mixolydian from C major?
questions.answer: C Mixolydian has B-flat rather than B-natural.

questions.prompt: Why might A-A-B-B still be binary?
questions.answer: It contains two principal sections, each repeated, rather than four distinct formal sections.
